title: Redwood discovery - reliability & fallback discussion with Helio Tech
summary: Discovery call to understand Helio Tech's reliability needs for LLM powered features. They run customer-facing conversational flows and need <100ms p95 for part of the traffic, multi-region failover, and strict audit/KMS controls. Discussed Redwood hosted + dedicated + private tradeoffs, model variant fallbacks, automatic routing, and SLA targets. Next steps: share security package, baseline latency numbers, and propose pilot config for dedicated pool + cross-region failover.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Samir from Redwood here, with Lena from our SE team. Good to meet you all.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Hi, thanks, Samir. Maya Chen, VP Eng at Helio Tech. We have Ravi and Talia on too.
[00:12] Ravi Kapoor: Hey.
[00:14] Talia Gomez: Morning.
[00:16] Samir Patel: Quick agenda — just to align: understand your reliability & incident tolerance requirements, current infra, and map to Redwood hosted/dedicated/private options + potential fallback strategies. Sound good?
[00:27] Alex Ruiz: Yep, sounds good.
[00:30] Lena Ortiz: Great. Maybe start with your stack — where are you running models today?
[00:35] Maya Chen: We have mixed setup. Most prod calls go to a managed vendor currently, some inference on prem for PII redaction. Latency is an issue, especially for synchronous flows. We need under ~100ms p95 for search/autocomplete but chat use can tolerate higher.
[00:52] Samir Patel: Got it. Are you looking at Redwood hosted, or would dedicated or private be required because of data residency?
[01:05] Maya Chen: Residency isn't the blocker, it's more about incident tolerance. Our customers pay for SLAs. If the vendor has an outage we need automatic fallback so the experience doesn't break. Example: serve a smaller model or degrade gracefully.
[01:25] Ravi Kapoor: Yeah, we had an incident last quarter where KV cache invalidation caused 30s tail latency spikes, and the vendor's failover required manual intervention. We want automated cross-region routing and a clear SLA.
[01:39] Lena Ortiz: Understood. For Redwood we have a few levers: routing policies, multi-region endpoints, model variant fallbacks (quantized models or CPU-based fallbacks), and canary/weighted routing for gradual rollouts. We also support route-level SLOs.
[01:58] Maya Chen: When you say model variant fallbacks, do you mean you can automatically switch to a smaller quantized variant if the primary is saturated?
[02:07] Lena Ortiz: Exactly — policy-driven. You can set thresholds by queue depth, latency, or error rates. When threshold is hit we route to a compatible variant — e.g., from 8-bit quantized GPU model to 4-bit, or to a CPU-hosted compact model.
[02:23] Ravi Kapoor: What's the expected failover time? We care about sub-1s for some flows, and up to 5s for others.
[02:32] Samir Patel: Failover is near-instant at the routing layer — usually a few hundred milliseconds for routing changes, but cold starts on a warmup can add seconds if a fallback requires spinning up capacity. To avoid that we recommend a warm standby or pre-warmed dedicated pool.
[02:49] Alex Ruiz: So dedicated pools reduce failover time because capacity is pre-reserved?
[02:54] Lena Ortiz: Yes. Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput and we can configure burst and warm standby policies. For strict SLOs we often see customers reserve a baseline dedicated pool in primary and secondary region.
[03:06] Maya Chen: How do you handle cross-region routing for GDPR and data residency? We can't cross certain regions for EU customers.
[03:14] Lena Ortiz: You can configure routing by region and customer attribute. For EU traffic we can pin to EU regions and still have a fallback within EU — e.g., fail from eu-west-1 to eu-central-1. For private deployments we can run the control plane in a customer VPC to meet stricter residency.
[03:31] Talia Gomez: Security question: KMS and audit logs — can we bring our own KMS/HSM and keep keys in our account?
[03:39] Samir Patel: For Private deployments yes, for Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS via IAM cross-account access; hosted can support customer-managed keys in many cases depending on contract. We also provide audit logs and token-level tracing in Redwood Console.
[03:55] Ravi Kapoor: What about SLA numbers? You mentioned route-level SLOs — what do you commit to?
[04:01] Lena Ortiz: Our published SLA for Dedicated customers is 99.95% availability with latency guardrails depending on model class. For hosted customers we have best-effort SLAs, but enterprise customers can get stronger terms. We can define error budgets and runbooks as part of an enterprise contract.
[04:20] Maya Chen: If we sign Dedicated, do we get cross-region redundancy out of the box or is that extra configuration?
[04:25] Samir Patel: It's an architecture decision — we can offer a multi-region deployment template as part of Dedicated. It typically involves reserved pools in each region and smart routing rules. We can include cross-region failover in the SLA if we own the deployment across those regions.
[04:40] Alex Ruiz: How do you test the fallbacks? Can we run synthetic traffic and chaos experiments?
[04:45] Lena Ortiz: Yes, we recommend a POC where we run bench tests and fault injection. We have a benchmark harness and a chaos playbook. We'll run baseline latency numbers and then simulate a regional outage and observe routing/fallback behavior.
[05:00] Ravi Kapoor: For our team, observability is key. Do you expose per-request traces and token-level latency so we can tie errors back to our app traces?
[05:08] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood Console provides tracing hooks, per-route dashboards, and token-level cost/latency breakdowns. You can pipeline logs to your SIEM and get audit trails.
[05:18] Talia Gomez: A question about stateful workloads: KV cache — if you fail to another region do you lose context?
[05:25] Lena Ortiz: By default KV cache is local to a region for latency reasons. For long session continuity we recommend session replication or sticky routing; or store session state in a global datastore and layer that with token prefix caching. For heavy state requirements a private deployment gives more control over replication.
[05:43] Maya Chen: Do you support gradual degradation strategies — like respond with a cached summary instead of invoking the model?
[05:50] Lena Ortiz: Yes — we support cache-first policies and application-level fallbacks. You can configure a policy that returns a cached answer or a simpler heuristic response during overload.
[05:59] Alex Ruiz: Regarding costs — warm standby and dedicated capacity costs more. We need to balance cost vs strict SLA. How do customers typically structure this?
[06:07] Samir Patel: Common pattern: critical synchronous traffic goes to a small dedicated pool with warm standby in a secondary region; less-critical chat goes to hosted with fallback to compact models. Redwood Optimize can give recommendations based on observed traffic.
[06:22] Ravi Kapoor: Any limits on model compatibility for fallbacks? Some fallback paths may not be semantically equivalent.
[06:29] Lena Ortiz: Right — model variant fallbacks are best-effort compatible; we recommend running evaluation tests to measure drift. You can set quality thresholds so if fallback deviates too far it will instead serve a graceful degrade message.
[06:42] Samir Patel: Quick check — what are your success criteria for a pilot?
[06:46] Maya Chen: We want to validate failover time under load (target <2s for critical paths), confirm audit/KMS integration, and measure latency p95 with dedicated warm pool. Also need a runbook that maps incidents to response steps.
[07:00] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. We can propose a two-week pilot: baseline benchmarks, simulated outage, and security integration.
[07:07] Alex Ruiz: That timeline works. Who will own the runbook?
[07:10] Maya Chen: Our SRE team will own it but we want Redwood to provide the template and the scripted tests.
[07:16] Samir Patel: We'll provide a runbook template and the benchmark harness. We'll also include a suggested Dedicated configuration.
[07:23] Ravi Kapoor: On the routing side, how granular is the policy? Can it be per-tenant?
[07:28] Lena Ortiz: Yes, per-route and per-tenant policies are supported. You can route high-tier customers to dedicated pools and others to hosted.
[07:36] Talia Gomez: For compliance we need retention controls on logs — can that be set per-customer?
[07:41] Samir Patel: Yes, retention and redaction policies are configurable — especially in Dedicated and Private deployments.
[07:48] Maya Chen: Any gotchas — network egress across regions?
[07:52] Lena Ortiz: Cross-region egress can increase costs and latency; it's configurable and we can model expected costs as part of the pilot.
[07:59] Alex Ruiz: Ok. Can you share a reference architecture for multi-region dedicated with failover?
[08:04] Samir Patel: We'll send the multi-region template and a sample traffic policy — link: https://redwood.ai/arch/multi-region-template (note: placeholder).
[08:16] Maya Chen: We also need SOC2 & ISO docs, and any pen test reports for Hosted.
[08:21] Samir Patel: We'll share security package: SOC2 Type II, ISO certs, pen test summary — link in follow-up.
[08:28] Ravi Kapoor: For the pilot, what telemetry should we collect?
[08:31] Lena Ortiz: Latency p50/p95/p99, queue depth, model latency breakdown, region failover times, error rates, and token-level costs.
[08:41] Alex Ruiz: When can we start the pilot? We are targeting an April eng sprint.
[08:46] Samir Patel: We can schedule provisioning the week of April 6th. We'll need a small SRE contact to run tests.
[08:54] Maya Chen: Ravi will be the SRE contact.
[08:56] Ravi Kapoor: Yep.
[08:57] Talia Gomez: One more — encryption at rest for private deployment — full disk?
[09:01] Samir Patel: Yes, private includes customer-managed KMS and encrypted volumes; we can show config details.
[09:06] Alex Ruiz: Great. Walk me through a sample incident scenario — primary region outage, what's the step-by-step?
[09:12] Lena Ortiz: Step 1: routing detects region health degradation via probes and increased error rates. Step 2: policy triggers routing to secondary region or fallback model. Step 3: if capacity isn't warm we spin warm standby; Step 4: console alerts and we run automated runbook steps. We can also fail to cache-first if configured.
[09:32] Maya Chen: How do you avoid split-brain or double-billing when routing changes?
[09:36] Samir Patel: We maintain request-level idempotency and token accounting in the control plane; billing is reconciled against routed region. We'll share details in the runbook.
[09:47] Alex Ruiz: Thanks. That was helpful.
[09:50] Samir Patel: Quick recap and next steps — I'll send the security package, multi-region template, and a proposed pilot config. Lena will send benchmark harness instructions. We'll aim to provision week of April 6.
[10:05] Maya Chen: Sounds good.
[10:07] Ravi Kapoor: Thanks everyone.
[10:09] Talia Gomez: Thanks.
[10:11] Samir Patel: End call.
